newsitem.title: MEXICO: Former Mexican military officers join opposition.
newsitem.headline: Former Mexican military officers join opposition.

text.p: Nearly a dozen retired high-ranking Mexican military officers publicly joined a leftist opposition party on Monday in a rare snub to the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party.

Ten retired army and navy officers, including generals and admirals, quit their memberships in the long-ruling PRI to join the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), the PRD said in a statement. One active naval officer also joined.

"Today, a group of retired high-ranking military officers ... decided to join the party's ranks in an effort to strengthen civil society and promote political change in the country," the PRD statement said.
Some of the ex-officers cited Mexico's recent economic crisis and corruption scandals as reasons for their decision.

"I am here (because of) the problems Mexico faces due to the lying, criminal, elitist, and rapacious government that Mexico suffered through between 1988 and 1994," said retired Brig. Gen. Samuel Lara Villa, one of the officers.

Villa was referring to the administration of disgraced former President Carlos Salinas, who fled Mexico shortly after his term amid an economic crisis and allegations of widespread corruption. Salinas has denied all wrongdoing.

Mexico's military has historically shunned the political spotlight and has been unswervingly devoted to the PRI, which took power shortly after the revolution and has held on since. Unlike other Latin American nations, Mexico has not been plagued in recent history by military unrest.
Although a handful of military officers have shown sympathy for the PRD since the party was formed in the late 1980s, few have made their sympathies public.

"This is a significant public demonstration and probably healthy for Mexico. It shows that military people have the right as individuals to not be tied to the PRI," said Roderic Camp, a political analyst at Tulane University and a leading expert on Mexico's armed forces.
However, Camp added the military could increasingly become a battleground among different political parties vying for influence in different sectors of society.
Three brigadier generals, one admiral, three vice admirals, and two rear admirals were among those who joined the PRD, Mexico's leading leftist opposition.
